output.title: When demo theatre quietly eats workflow time
output.body:
If you run a small business and you have already tried ChatGPT, the trap is easy to spot: you spend good time on polished demos, POCs, or “one more tool” tests, but the real workflow keeps waiting. That is the quiet cost of demo theatre.

The practical question is not whether the demo looks clever. It is whether you have one recurring workflow that keeps coming back and produces something you can measure. In the kind of small-business scenario Bareni works with, that can look like repeated customer questions, manual invoice or data work, or follow-ups that never stop. If the work is not repeating, AI is probably not the place to start. No drama there.

Bareni’s diagnostic is deliberately bounded: identify one recurring workflow, check honestly whether AI fits, and if it does, define a fixed-price pilot with clear measures. There is no mandatory roadmap gate in the middle. Pilot timing and scope are intended, not guaranteed. For customers who want strategy only, a separate AI Strategy & Roadmap exists.

We also keep scope discipline. Current exclusions include high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work; bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. That is current scope discipline, not a claim that such work can never be automated.

A good next step is simple: ask yourself whether you have one repeating workflow that reliably eats about 5–10 hours a week, with an output you can measure and a human still approving the risky part. If not, the demo is probably not the thing to optimise.
